h1: SEO for study abroad and immigration consultants
metaTitle: SEO for Study Abroad Consultants in India
metaDescription: Demand is reset by other governments' visa policy. The model is maintenance, not volume: destination pages rewritten within days beat fifty new posts.
answer: Aggregators own the head terms and the local pack is decided by an address, so neither is worth buying. What a consultancy can win is destination by course by intake by eligibility — pages narrow enough that nobody else maintains them, rewritten within days when a visa or PR rule changes. Maintenance beats volume here, consistently.
takeaways: Your demand curve belongs to other governments. A dependant rule or a permit cap announced in another country resets your enquiry mix before your next content calendar is even approved.
The winnable matrix is smaller than it looks — for most Indian consultancies, **40 to 120 destination pages**, not six hundred. Eligibility variants are sections inside a page, not separate URLs.
The rewrite trigger matters more than the publishing calendar. A page updated within 72 hours of a policy change outperforms fifty new posts written the same quarter.
`best study abroad consultant in <city>` is decided by proximity and reviews. Get the profile right, then stop spending content money on it.
A 90-day baseline is unusually checkable in this industry, because an intake deadline either passed with more applications submitted or it didn't.

sections.h2: Your demand curve belongs to other governments
body: Almost every industry we write for has a demand curve set by its own market. Yours is set by immigration ministries in four or five countries that have never heard of you, and it can move in a single announcement.

The concrete version: [the UK now permits dependants only for government-sponsored students on courses longer than six months, or full-time postgraduate students on research degrees](https://www.gov.uk/student-visa/family-members). Read that as a marketer rather than a lawyer and it says something specific — the married applicant in their late twenties, who was a large part of the UK enquiry mix, stopped being a UK applicant and became somebody else's applicant. Every destination has had at least one change of that magnitude in recent years, in both directions.

This has two consequences that most consultancies' content plans ignore entirely. First, a page about a destination is a perishable asset, not a permanent one. Second, the traffic doesn't disappear when the rule changes — it converts into a different query, usually a worried one, and whoever answers that query within the week collects the enquiry.

callout.title: The best-timed page you will ever publish
callout.body: When a destination tightens, the searches that spike are "is <country> still worth it", "what changed", "which alternative accepts my profile". Those searchers are not browsing — they had a plan and it broke. A calm, dated, accurate page published inside a week converts better than anything you'll write on a normal Tuesday.

sections.h2: The page matrix, and how large it should actually be
body: The instinct is to build every combination. Ten destinations, twenty course families, three intakes, eight profile variants and you have a project plan for 4,800 pages, none of which anybody will ever maintain. That is [scaled content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) with a spreadsheet behind it, and the penalty lands on the domain rather than on the thin pages.
Build the matrix from what you actually place students into, and cap it at the number one person can genuinely re-verify in the week after a policy change.

rows: Only countries you have placed students into and can name universities for. A destination page with no placements behind it reads exactly as thin as it is

September or Fall, January or Spring, and May where it exists. The intake changes deadlines, funding and accommodation — that's enough to justify a URL
Backlogs, gaps, low scores, no test taken, work experience — these are **sections inside** the destination page, answered honestly. Splitting them into URLs is where consultancies get flagged

bullets: That multiplies out to roughly **40 to 120 real pages** for most Indian consultancies. Fewer than you were sold, and more than you currently maintain.
Each page needs a visible verified-on date and one named owner. If no one owns it, it shouldn't exist.
Write the eligibility sections as questions in the applicant's own words — 'I have four backlogs, can I apply' outperforms 'Academic Requirements' by a distance.
Fees, living costs and funding requirements go on the page as ranges with the source and the date, never as a single number you'll forget to change.
A separate page per city office is fine. A separate page per city for the same destination is the doorway pattern, and Google names it explicitly.

sections.h2: Maintenance beats volume, and the rewrite trigger is the whole system
body: Most content retainers in this industry are sold as output — twelve posts a month, a blog calendar, a quarterly report of words shipped. For a study abroad consultancy that's close to the wrong product. The asset that produces enquiries is a set of pages that are correct today, and correctness decays on somebody else's schedule.
So build the trigger, not just the calendar.
numbered: **Name the official source per destination.** The immigration department's own news or updates page, not an aggregator's newsletter and not a WhatsApp forward. One URL per country, checked weekly, and read by a person.

**Set a service level in hours, not sprints.** A material policy change means the affected destination pages are updated within 48 to 72 hours. Not a new blog post announcing it — the standing page rewritten, with the old position noted and dated.

**Stamp the change on the page.** 'Updated on <date> to reflect <what changed>' at the top. It's the honest thing, and it's also the line that makes a returning searcher trust you over a page they can't date.

**Push for a recrawl, then be patient.** Resubmit the sitemap and use URL Inspection on the important pages — but [Google is explicit that recrawling can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks, and that requesting a crawl guarantees nothing](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/ask-google-to-recrawl). That lag is the argument for having the page already ranking before the news breaks.
**Retire what you can't maintain.** A destination you stopped placing into is a liability. Redirect it or take it down rather than leaving a wrong page ranking under your name.

callout.title: The wrong page that ranks is the expensive one
callout.body: An outdated visa or eligibility page doesn't just underperform — a family plans around it, discovers the rule changed eighteen months ago, and the complaint arrives at your office rather than at Google's. In a business built entirely on trust with parents, one of those costs more than a quarter of content.

sections.h2: Why we won't sell you 'best study abroad consultant in Pune'
body: It's the query every consultancy asks for and it's the one we decline to promise, for a reason that has nothing to do with effort. Google's local results are decided largely by relevance, distance and prominence, which in practice means an office address, a category and a review profile. You cannot write your way past a competitor whose office is two kilometres closer to the searcher, and no agency that tells you otherwise is planning to explain that in month four.

That doesn't mean ignoring it. It means treating it as hygiene rather than as a content programme — which is exactly the [distinction between a ranking promise and an outcome](/journal/why-ranking-guarantees-are-a-lie) we make everywhere else on this site.
bullets: **Do the profile work once, properly.** Correct category, real photos of the office, actual counselling hours, the languages your counsellors speak, and a Q&A seeded with the questions you're asked on every call.

**Ask every admitted student for a review**, once, at the point the visa lands. Never incentivise it and never filter to the happy ones — both break Google's policy and both are visible to the parent reading them.
**Reply to the bad review carefully.** In this industry a complaint usually involves a refusal. Never discuss a specific case publicly, and never blame the student.
**Then move the budget.** A destination page ranks for a searcher in any city. A locality page ranks for the people already walking past your board.

sections.h2: Where the aggregators are weak, and where they aren't
body: Yocket, Leverage Edu, IDP and Shiksha have spent years building university databases, ranking pages and generic destination guides. On `MS in USA` or `universities in Canada for Indian students`, you're competing against a database and a decade of links. Concede those in the first meeting and the plan improves immediately.
What none of them do well is the specific, the recent and the uncomfortable — because a database updates on a release cycle and a counsellor updates on a phone call.
bullets: **Post-change explainers, fast.** They will publish something eventually. You can publish it on the day, from the destination pages you already maintain.

**Documentation as it actually works in India.** Transcripts from a state university, apostille and attestation, financial documents a specific consulate wants, education loan sanction letters, gap affidavits. Enormous search volume, almost entirely answered by forum threads.

**Refusal and reapplication content.** `<country> student visa refusal reasons`, `can I reapply after refusal`. Aggregators avoid it because it doesn't read as aspirational. It's read by people in genuine distress who will call somebody that afternoon.

**Profile-honest eligibility.** What a three-year degree, a low score, a five-year gap or four backlogs actually means for each destination — including where the honest answer is 'this destination is not for you, try that one'. That page earns trust nothing else buys.
**Cost of living in a specific city**, with the currency and the month stated, rather than a country-level average that was never true of anywhere.

**Your own name.** `<consultancy> reviews`, `<consultancy> fees`, `is <consultancy> genuine`. If a forum thread from 2021 answers that query, it is answering it for every parent who checks you out. That page is the highest-return thing on the whole site and it takes a fortnight.

sections.h2: Measure against the intake, not the month — and what this costs
body: Here's the part that makes this industry easier to be honest in than most. A rolling monthly report is a poor instrument for a business with two or three deadlines a year. An intake is a hard edge: applications were either submitted before it closed or they weren't, and no dashboard can argue with that.

So we set the baseline the same way we always do — your trailing-90-day count of qualified organic enquiries, frozen on day one — but we agree upfront which 90 days matter. For a September intake, the decisive window is roughly the previous November to February, when applications and funding documents are actually going out. A quarter ending in July proves very little about anything, in either direction.

And the counted event has to be an event your counsellors work: a booked counselling session, a profile evaluation form, an application actually submitted. Not sessions, and not the ebook downloads that any of us could inflate in a fortnight without placing a single student.

A single-office consultancy working three or four destinations sits at our ₹40,000 a month tier. A multi-branch firm covering seven or eight destinations with an intake calendar and a maintenance obligation is ₹75,000 and up, because the work is genuinely more surface to keep correct. Ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, and you keep every asset. Full numbers on [pricing](/pricing); the wider market range is on [what SEO costs in India](/cost/seo-cost-in-india).

Miss the agreed baseline in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it. We never promise a specific ranking position, because nobody controls Google's index — and a firm that spends its day telling students not to trust guaranteed-admission promises should be the first to recognise the shape of the argument.

callout.title: What ninety days can and cannot cover
callout.body: Brand-query defence and documentation content often move inside six to ten weeks, because the competition is thin and you hold the knowledge. Destination and course pages against the aggregators take two to three quarters. A policy-change page can rank in days, but only if the destination page it hangs off is already trusted — which is the argument for building in the quiet months rather than the news cycle.

faqs.q: Can a study abroad consultancy outrank Yocket, Leverage Edu or IDP?
faqs.a: Not on database queries like `universities in Canada for Indian students` — that's a decade of links and a structured dataset. You win on the specific and the recent: documentation as it works in India, refusal and reapplication content, profile-honest eligibility, city-level living costs, and post-policy explainers published within days rather than on a release cycle.

faqs.q: How many destination pages should we actually build?
faqs.a: For most Indian consultancies, 40 to 120. Four to eight destinations you genuinely place into, two to four course families, two or three intakes — and eligibility variants written as sections inside those pages rather than as separate URLs. Cap it at what one person can re-verify in the week after a policy change.

faqs.q: How quickly should pages be updated after a visa rule changes?
faqs.a: Within 48 to 72 hours, on the standing destination page rather than as a new blog post, with a dated note saying what changed. Then resubmit the sitemap and inspect the key URLs — though Google is explicit that recrawling takes days to weeks, which is why the page needs to already be ranking before the news lands.

faqs.q: Is 'best study abroad consultant in my city' worth targeting?
faqs.a: As profile hygiene, yes. As a content programme, no. Local results are driven largely by proximity, category and reviews, so a competitor two kilometres closer to the searcher has an advantage you can't write past. Do the Business Profile properly, collect reviews honestly, then spend the content budget on destination pages that rank for any city.

faqs.q: Should we publish our consultancy fees?
faqs.a: Publish a band with what it includes — profile evaluation, applications, SOP support, visa filing, and what's charged separately. Parents search it either way, and a forum thread with a guessed number is currently answering for you. Expect fewer enquiries and a materially higher proportion that survive the first call.

faqs.q: How do you measure SEO for a business with only two or three intakes a year?
faqs.a: Against the intake, not the month. Freeze qualified organic enquiries — booked counselling sessions, profile evaluations, applications submitted — and agree in writing which 90-day window is being compared, usually the same window a year earlier. A quarter that contains no application deadline proves almost nothing either way.
